subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Art of Good Enough: When to Stop Deciding
description: A quick win: understand The Art of Good Enough: When to Stop Deciding.

hook.text: You compare 47 restaurants, read 200 reviews, & spend an hour choosing dinner. Was the extra research worth it?

twist.text: The time & energy spent finding the 'best' option is itself a cost.

punchline.text: Good enough is often great enough. Perfection is the enemy of done.

quiz.question: What did Schwartz discover about maximizers vs. satisficers?
options: Maximizers make objectively better choices but are less happy with them

details.summary: Satisficing means choosing the first option that meets your minimum criteria rather than exhaustively searching for the best one. Herbert Simon showed that in complex environments, satisficing often produces better outcomes than maximizing.
details.whyItMatters: Perfectionist maximizing wastes time and causes decision fatigue. Knowing when good enough is good enough preserves energy for decisions that truly matter.
takeaways: Satisficing chooses the first option that clears a threshold
Maximizing searches exhaustively but often leads to less satisfaction
Herbert Simon coined 'satisficing' and won the Nobel Prize for it

faq.question: What is the difference between satisficing and just being lazy?
faq.answer: Satisficing deliberately sets criteria, then stops searching once they are met. Laziness avoids setting criteria and avoids searching at all. Satisficing is a strategic decision about how to allocate limited decision-making resources.

faq.question: When should you maximize instead of satisficing?
faq.answer: Maximize for irreversible high-stakes decisions where the difference between options is large and consequential. Satisfice for frequent, reversible, lower-stakes choices where the search cost exceeds the likely improvement.
